**On Islands That Were Never There**

For roughly a century and a half, maps of the Pacific showed a sliver of land in the Coral Sea, northwest of New Caledonia, called Sandy Island. It appeared on British Admiralty charts. It appeared in the *Times Atlas of the World*. It appeared, as late as 2012, on Google Earth, a dark elongated smudge in an otherwise unbroken field of blue. In November of that year an Australian research vessel, the *Southern Surveyor*, sailed to the coordinates to have a look. The crew found water 1,400 meters deep. There was no island. There had never been an island. Someone—probably the crew of a whaling ship in 1876—had recorded something, a pumice raft perhaps, or a low bank of cloud, and the record had simply propagated forward, chart to chart, atlas to atlas, for 136 years, because no one had a reason to check.

I find I can't stop thinking about this, and about the family of such places that cartographers now call phantom islands. There are dozens of them. Hy-Brasil sat off the west coast of Ireland on maps from 1325 until the 1870s, sometimes drawn as a perfect circle bisected by a channel, said to be visible only one day every seven years. Frisland, a large and detailed island south of Iceland with named towns and promontories, was invented—or hallucinated, or fabricated—by a Venetian named Nicolò Zeno in 1558 and copied faithfully by Mercator and Ortelius, the two best mapmakers alive. Saint Brendan's Isle drifted around the Atlantic for centuries, wherever there happened to be space for it. Bermeja, a small island in the Gulf of Mexico that appeared on Spanish charts from the 1500s, mattered enough that in 2009 the Mexican government sent an expedition to find it, because its existence would have extended their claim to undersea oil. It was not there either.

What interests me is not that people made mistakes. Of course they did; the sea is enormous and ships are small and a fogbank at dusk looks very much like a coastline. What interests me is the persistence. A phantom island is an error that has learned to survive. It gets copied because it is on the previous map, and the previous map was made by someone reputable, and the person copying has no way to verify and no incentive to omit. Leaving a known island off a chart could sink a ship. Leaving a nonexistent one on costs nothing, or seems to. So the safe move, for generation after generation of mapmakers, is to keep the island. Error becomes tradition. Tradition becomes fact.

Some of these islands had teeth. The Isle of Demons, placed near Newfoundland on sixteenth-century maps, was reported to be full of screaming spirits; sailors said you could hear them from the deck. In 1542 a French noblewoman named Marguerite de La Rocque was marooned on an island in that region as punishment for an affair, and survived two years there, and the island she survived on may or may not have been the one the maps meant—the story and the geography have been tangled ever since. The Mountains of Kong, a range that stretched across West Africa on maps for almost a hundred years, existed because a respected geographer named James Rennell drew them in 1798, extrapolating from a traveler's vague report of hills. Explorers planned routes around them. Schoolchildren learned them. In 1889 a French officer named Louis-Gustave Binger walked to where they should have been and found flat savannah, and the mountains vanished from the next edition, and that was that.

The Arctic produced the most poignant ones, because there the illusion had physical help. Fata Morgana—a mirage created when layers of air at different temperatures bend light—can lift the distant ice into towers and ridges that look exactly like land. In 1906, Robert Peary stood on a cape in northern Greenland and saw, far to the northwest, snowy peaks he named Crocker Land after his financial backer. Seven years later Donald MacMillan led an expedition specifically to reach it. His party marched across the sea ice for days toward mountains they could see perfectly well, mountains that receded as they approached and then, when the sun shifted, dissolved. MacMillan wrote that his Inuit guide, Piugaattoq, had told him from the start that it was *poo-jok*—mist—and that he had not believed him. There is a whole essay in that sentence, about whose knowledge counts and whose does not, but I will let it stand on its own.

Why do I love these places? Partly for the comedy of it, the image of a scholarly man in Antwerp carefully inking in the harbors of a country that no one had ever seen. Partly because they are a kind of fossil record of hope: people wanted there to be land out there, wanted the blank spaces filled, and so the spaces got filled with whatever was nearest to hand. But mostly I think I love them because they are a clean, bounded example of something that is usually too diffuse to see. Every field has its Sandy Islands—the study everyone cites that no one has read, the etymology that is repeated because it is charming, the fact that is a fact because it was in the previous edition. Most of them will never get a research vessel sent to their coordinates. Most of them sit in deep water, unexamined, and do no obvious harm, which is exactly why they persist.

There is a small, quiet pleasure in the moment of correction. The *Southern Surveyor*'s log for that day is not dramatic. Someone noted the depth. Someone noted the absence. Then they sailed on, and a few months later the smudge disappeared from the map, and the Coral Sea got a little bit truer, and a little bit emptier. I think about how many things I believe that are like Sandy Island—inherited, plausible, unverified, drawn in by someone I'll never meet—and I hope that when the vessel finally arrives, I will have the grace to look at the open water and simply write down what is there.
